articles.title: Bob Dylan banket på pavens dør – og ble tatt imot
articles.content:
Låtskriveren, sangeren og poeten Bob Dylan har besøkt pave Leo i Vatikanstaten i en pause mellom konserter i Italia.

Vatikanet opplyser at møtet onsdag var kortfattet. Paven ga Dylan en rosenkrans, mens Dylan overrakte et eksemplar av selvbiografien sin, «Chronicles: Volume One», til paven.

Dylan, som vant Nobelprisen i litteratur i 2016, var kledd i svart hettegenser og et løst slips. Bilder fra Vatikanet viste ham med hetten trukket over hodet under møtet.

Dette var ikke Dylans første pavemøte. I 1997 spilte han for pave Johannes Paul og tusenvis av tilskuere under en kongress i Bologna i Italia.

Dylan ble født inn i en jødisk familie i Minnesota. Han ble en profilert nyfrelst kristen i 1979. I nyere tid har Dylan vært mer tilbakeholden om sitt religiøse syn. I et intervju med Wall Street Journal i 2022 sa han at han var en religiøs person som leser de hellige skriftene, mediterer og ber.

Paven og Vatikanet

Pave Frans døde 2. påskedag 2025, 88 år gammel.
Torsdag 8.mai ble Robert Francis Prevost (69) valgt til pave. Han tok Leo XIV til navn.

articles.content:
– For at folk som kunne ha de samme mulighetene til å reise som før og kunne komme seg rundt uten å bruke bilen, så øker vi antallet elsykler, sier byrådsleder Eirik Lae Solberg (H) til VG.

Det totale taket for elektriske utleiekjøretøy forblir på 16.000, men antallet elsparkesykler kuttes fra 16.000 til maksimalt 12.000. De resterende 4000 plassene settes av til elsykler når byrådet nå lyser ut ny anbudskonkurranse.

Byrådet setter også en fast nedre aldersgrense på 16 år for både elsykler og elsparkesykler.

– Vi hever aldersgrensen til 16 år sånn at vi styrker tryggheten både for dem som bruker elsykler- og elsparkesykler og for fotgjengere, sier Solberg.

Elsykkel og elsparkesykkel

Titusenvis av elsparkesykler er utplassert i norske byer, og legevaktene melder om mange ulykker. I Oslo har kommunen satt et tak på 16.000 elsparkesykler.

                        Norway urged to step up anti-discrimination efforts, fewer young immigrants outside work, a record-warm October, and more news this Wednesday.

Council of Europe calls on Norway to step up anti-discrimination efforts

A new report from the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI), a human rights group under the Council of Europe, urges Norway to do more to fight hate speech and hate crime, with a focus on equal treatment and inclusion in education and healthcare, as reported on their website.

While the commission praised some progress since its 2021 report, such as creating a hate-crime unit in the Oslo police and hiring multilingual staff in kindergartens and schools, it also issued 12 formal recommendations for Norway.

They designated two top priorities which should be addressed in the next 18 months. First, authorities are urged to build a culture of "living together" in schools to fight racism, bullying, growing antisemitism, anti-Muslim racism, and LGBTI intolerance. Second, ECRI called fora national plan to ensure all minority groups have equal access to healthcare.

The ECRI report also raised concerns about discrimination against Roma and Romani people, delays in care for transgender individuals, among others, and suggested that victims of discrimination should get free legal help.

These findings match local surveys that show discrimination within the system. The multicultural newspaper Utrop reported that in a survey about Oslo Municipality services, 38.9 percent of people who dealt with schools or educational institutions in the past year felt they were treated worse because of their skin colour, ethnic background, or religion.

Norwegian vocabulary: diskriminering - discrimination

Fewer young immigrants outside work and education in Norway

The proportion of young immigrants in Norway, aged 20 to 39, who are neither in employment nor education has fallen over the past decade, according to new data from Statistics Norway (SSB).

From 2015 to 2025, this share dropped from 32 percent to 26 percent, marking a bigger decrease than in the general population.

The drop was even bigger for Norwegian-born youth with immigrant parents. Their exclusion rate fell to 16.8 percent, getting closer to the 11.7 percent rate for those without an immigrant background.

Only Eastern European immigrants saw an increase, rising to 30.6 percent, which SSB attributes to the high number of Ukrainian refugees arriving since 2022.

The report also pointed out a clear gender gap. Among first-generation immigrants, women are excluded from work or education more often than men (29.1 percent compared to 23.7 percent), even though women usually have more education.

However, for second-generation youth born in Norway, the pattern is reversed. Young women have lower exclusion rates than young men (14.9 percent versus 18.5 percent) and are more included in work and education.

The Norwegian Meteorological Institute reported that this October was the third warmest ever, with temperatures 2.7C above normal. Only two years have been warmer: 2000 and 1901.

"We see that autumn is getting warmer and warmer. Average temperatures are rising, and we are getting more days above 15C. Autumn will of course always be unpredictable, but over time it will still become both warmer and wetter," climate researcher Reidun Gangstø said in a press release.

Although it has been generally warm throughout the country, the north stands out the most. Some areas in Nordland, northern Troms, and Finnmark were "extremely warm". For example, Svalbard Airport had a record high of 10.2C, very unusual for the time of the year.

Bird flu detected in 7,500 chickens in western Norway

The Norwegian Food Safety Authority said on Tuesday that bird flu was found in 7,500 chickens on a farm in Klepp, Rogaland, confirming the H5N1 virus.

A three-kilometre protection zone was set up around the farm, and all birds had to be culled after the outbreak.

The avian influenza virus is highly pathogenic, meaning it causes severe illness and high mortality rates among all types of birds. However, it can rarely spread to mammals and humans, which is why the food safety authority said it is highly unlikely to get the virus from eating eggs or poultry meat.

"Avian influenza is a very serious disease in birds. In order to limit the spread of infection and safeguard animal welfare, we have decided to euthanise all birds in the flock," department head Jarle Bergsjø said in a press release.

Authorities will also test 13 other farms near the affected site, while restriction zones and surveillance measures have been introduced across several municipalities, including Stavanger, Randaberg, Sola, Sandnes (except former Forsand), Klepp, Time, and Hå.

                        Our latest Norwegian word of the day can be surprisingly useful

Today’s word of the day is nyttig. Nyttig traces its origins from the Old Norse word nyttogher and has existed in its current form for centuries in Norway. It also exists and is used in Danish and Swedish.

It has a number of different meanings, but is most often used to mean “useful”. For example, “jeg vil gjøre meg nyttig”, (I’d like to make myself useful) or “trening er nyttig for kroppen,” (working out is good for the body).

However, useful isn’t always meant in the most positive of lights. That’s because nyttig is linked to the verb å nytte (to make use of), which you’ll see related to the word utnytte (to exploit or take advantage of).

You could, for example, say that a certain skill, experience or piece of information is nyttig (useful), and the English phrase "useful idiot", describing someone who can easily be manipulated, translates into Norwegian as nyttig idiot.

If you want a synonym for nyttig which is less ambiguous, brukbar and anvendelig (both “usable”) make good substitutes.

The opposite of nyttig is unyttig, which can be used to describe something useless. Likewise, ubrukelig from the verb å bruke (to use) also means "useless".

                        Speaking at a national integration conference in Oslo, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre pointed out that more than 21 percent of people in Norway now have an immigrant background, calling for unity and embracing diversity.

Norwegian ​PM Støre delivered an opening speech at the annual conference of the Directorate of Integration and Diversity (Integrerings- og mangfoldsdirektoratet, or IMDi) in Oslo, declaring that Norway’s growing diversity is now a key part of the country’s identity.

Støre talked about how Norway’s population has changed over the last sixty years, comparing the country he grew up in to today’s society:

"I was born in 1960. You can do the math yourselves, and in the census that year, there were 62,500 foreign-born people living in Norway. That was 1.7 percent of the population. Today, I am 66, and the total immigrant population is over 1.2 million—21.7 percent of the population.

"Out of these 1.2 million, 238,000 are Norwegian-born with an immigrant background, and 340,000 are individuals with a refugee background; that is, from 62,000 to 1.2 million. That is fundamental. And I think one of the most important things is that this is Norway, and this is who we are" he said.

Støre emphasised that immigration should not be seen as a contest between the majority and minority groups, referencing King Harald V's iconic 2016 speech on inclusivity: "The most important thing we must do in our minds is realise that this is not an exercise of 'us versus them'—between a majority population and a minority population—because we are our country. I think King Harald phrased it very well when he said that this is us in Norway, all of us together. We share these tasks together, and we face our challenges together."

The speech comes during a turbulent period, as immigration is a major topic of debate both in Norway and across Europe.

Friction over integration is particularly evident in current national budget talks, the rising support for the right-wing Progress Party (FrP), whose leader recently called for stricter immigration controls, and an increasingly polarising climate where several politicians with an immigrant background are quitting or considering quitting due to online harassment.

You can watch the video of the speech on the website of the newspaper Nettavisen.

articles.title: Rødt vil øke skattene med 34 milliarder
articles.content:
Rødt legger i dag frem sitt alternative statsbudsjett, hvor det kommer frem hvordan de ville styrt om partiet hadde makten alene.

De vil blant annet øke formuesskatten med 16 milliarder og ha økt skatt på utbytte.

– De foreslåtte endringene øker skatteinntektene, inkludert utbytteskatt, med omtrent 34 milliarder kroner i 2027, sammenlignet med regjeringens forslag, står det i budsjettet.

Samtidig sier Rødt at partiets modell ville gitt lavere skatt for alle med under 800.000 kroner i inntekt.

De vil også kutte i momsen på mat 15 til 10 prosent fra juli neste år. Partiet vil også fryse norgespris på strøm på 40 øre, pluss moms. Regjeringen har foreslått en økning til 45 øre.

Regjeringen er avhengig av Rødt for å få flertall for sitt budsjett. Forhandlingene starter fredag.

Partiet Rødt

Partiet Rødt ble stiftet i mars 2007 på grunnlag av Rød Valgallianse og AKP, med Rød ungdom som ungdomsorganisasjon. I 2025 gjorde partiet sitt beste valg noensinne, med 5,3 prosent oppslutning.

                        Immigrants make up 57 percent of those on social assistance in Norway, ministers warn labour shortages threaten the economy, the Progress Party hits a record poll high, and more news this Tuesday.

Labour shortages pose biggest threat to Norway's economy

In an interview with Norwegian newspaper Aftenposten, Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg and Minister of Labour and Social Inclusion Kjersti Stenseng warned that Norway's working-age population has stopped growing for the first time since the Black Death.

Stoltenberg said Norway has reached a turning point. "The biggest threat to the Norwegian economy is a shortage of labour. And the most important thing we can do for Norwegian companies is to facilitate more people getting jobs," Stoltenberg told Aftenposten.

"For many years, the part of the population that is of working age has grown. But now the growth is levelling off, and eventually it will stop completely," he added.

Since most future population growth will come from people aged 75 and older, the ministers said more people need to join the workforce while those already employed will need to work more.

Stenseng also pointed out that roughly 700,000 people in Norway currently remain outside employment and education, highlighting that employment rates among residents with an immigrant background remain significantly lower than the rest of the population.

In response, the government is planning a 6.4 billion kroner income tax cut (which has sparked criticism for benefiting higher earners) alongside welfare reforms designed to encourage more people to get into the workforce.

Immigrants make up 57 percent of those receiving social assistance in Norway

According to a report from the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV), 164,300 people received social assistance for at least one month in 2025, representing 3.6 percent of the population. Nearly 92,800 of them had an immigrant background, making up about 57 percent.

When it comes to overall spending, 12.3 billion kroner was paid out in social assistance across the year, with 74 percent of payments going to immigrants. NAV report explained that most of this spending was due to longer support periods for recently arrived refugees, especially Ukrainians.

The figures also show that immigrants from Africa, Asia, Eastern Europe outside the EU, South and Central America, and parts of Oceania made up the largest group of foreign-born residents receiving assistance.

In contrast, only a few people from the EU and other Western countries like the UK and the US, who mostly come as labour migrants, needed social assistance. They made up just 54 million kroner of the total spending.

Nevertheless, overall spending stopped growing in 2025 because fewer new refugees arrived and more people who came in 2022 and 2023 found jobs.

Norwegian vocabulary: sosialhjelpsmottakerne - recipients of social assistance

Government committee proposes major healthcare shake-up

Last week, the government announced plans for Norway's biggest healthcare overhaul in 25 years, while waiting for formal recommendations from an expert commission.

On Monday, the government-appointed health committee shared its findings after a year-long review, warning that an ageing population, labour shortages, and more complex patient needs mean the system requires major changes, as reported by Aftenposten and newspaper VG.

The proposals suggest removing the four regional health authorities so the state would run hospitals directly and cutting the number of local health trusts from 20 to between 10 and 15.

The commission also recommended smaller municipalities should merge to deal with ongoing medical staff shortages

Besides changing how things are run, the experts suggested improving mental health services and making it easier to get care online. This includes offering 24/7 online medical advice.

The 472-page report has been sent for a three-month public consultation period before the government presents the formal proposalto parliament.

At Monday's presentation, Health Minister Jan Christian Vestre also provided some figures about the health system, highlighting that Norwegian hospitals treat almost three million patients each year and have nearly 150,000 staff. Municipalities care for 400,000 people, and GPs hold over 17 million consultations every year.

Right-wing Progress Party hits record high in new poll

Norway’s right-wing Progress Party (FrP) has reached its highest level of support, building a big lead on the political right, according to a new Verian poll for broadcaster TV 2.

The party rose to 32.2 percent, increasing its lead over Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre’s Labour Party, which is in second place at 22.9 percent.

At the same time, the Conservative Party (Høyre) dropped to just 13.1 percent, its lowest score since July 2009.

"Almost half of those who voted for the Conservative Party last autumn have now either sat on the fence or fled to other parties," said TV 2 election analyst Terje Sørensen.

The poll also showed changes for smaller parties. The Red Party went up by 1.1 points to 8.1 percent, while the Christian Democratic Party (KrF) fell to 2.7 percent.

articles.title: SV med 32 milliarder i økt skatt
articles.content:
Skattene økes med mer enn 32 milliarder kroner i helårseffekt i SVs alternative statsbudsjett.

I tillegg økes avgiftene med rundt 3,2 milliarder kroner i helårseffekt. Det er hovedsakelig klimaavgifter som økes. SV finner også rom til å fjerne dokumentavgiften for førstegangskjøpere av bolig.

Isolert for budsjettåret 2027 foreslår SV samlede skatte- og avgiftsøkninger på 25,6 milliarder.

Hovedforklaringen er en økning i formuesskatten på mer enn 16 milliarder kroner. Inntektsskatten økes med mer 3,2 milliarder, men SV sier to av tre vil få lavere skatt med deres opplegg.

– Skattenivået i dag er 24 milliarder kroner lavere i 2013 da Jens Stoltenberg sist var statsminister, sa finanspolitisk talsperson Marthe Hammer da hun la fram SV-budsjettet.

SV alternative budsjett legger opp til å bruke 309 millioner kroner mindre i oljepengebruk. En av satsingene er 10 milliarder kroner mer til kommunene, men bare 4 av milliardene gis som frie midler.

articles.title: IN DATA: Who were the 5,000 foreigners deported from Norway last year?
articles.content:

                        As well as tracking how many people move to Norway, the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) also monitors foreign nationals ordered to leave the country (with British citizens throwing up a surprise).

In 2025, Norwegian authorities issued formal deportation orders (utvisningsvedtak) to 5,002 foreign nationals, according to statistics from UDI.

A deportation order in Norway carries a formal entry ban, which prevents the person from returning to Norway for a certain period, or permanently in serious cases. It can even include a ban from entering the Schengen Area.

One of the main reasons a foreign resident can be deported from Norway is breaking the Immigration Act. This includes administrative violations like overstaying a visa, working without a valid permit, giving false information on residency applications, or not leaving the country after an asylum or visa refusal.

In 2025, 4,125 orders (which represents 82.5 percent of the total deportation orders) were issued on these grounds.

Foreign nationals can also be expelled from Norway after a criminal conviction, but this is much less common. Last year there were 368 such cases (7.4 percent of all deportation orders).

Contrary to popular belief, EU citizens are not exempt from being expelled from Norway, even though they have freedom of movement under the EEA Agreement.

In 2025, 500 orders (10 percent of all cases) were issued to European nationals. This can happen on grounds such as public order, public security, or abuse of rights.

In 2025, most deportation orders were given to nationals from South Asia and West Africa.

India had the highest number of cases with 949 in total. Of these, 941 were for immigration breaches and eight for criminal convictions. Pakistan was next with 918 orders, 917 for immigration breaches and one for a criminal conviction.

There was then a sharp drop. Bangladesh came third with 331 orders (329 for immigration breaches and two for criminal offences), and Nigeria in fourth place with 227 orders (218 for immigration breaches and nine for criminal convictions).

Combined, nationals from these four countries made up nearly 49 percent of all deportation orders in Norway in 2025.

Further down the overall list among non-EEA states were countries like Kenya with 112, Nepal (139), Ghana (111), China (78), the UK (62), Ukraine (59), and the United States with 42.

Australia and Canada recorded just 8 and 10 orders, respectively.

Among the European nationals, the highest number of expulsion orders was issued to citizens from Romania (160), Lithuania (89), Poland (75), and neighbouring Sweden (64), followed by the Netherlands (20), Latvia (13), and Spain (12).

UK nationals top list of convicted criminals deported

The figures show an unexpected trend in criminal deportations. Of the 62 British citizens ordered to leave in 2025, 35 were deported after criminal convictions. This made the UK the country with the most convicted criminals deported from Norway last year, ahead of Ukraine (33), China (31), and the United States (19).

A further 25 Britons were expelled for immigration status violations after losing EU freedom of movement post-Brexit.

READ ALSO: Indians, Brits and Syrians top Norway's permanent residency list

UDI statistics show a steady increase in expulsions in recent years.

Norwegian authorities recorded 1,210 deportation orders in 2021, 1,894 in 2022, 2,893 in 2023, and 3,302 in 2024. With the total passing the 5,000 mark in 2025, expulsion orders were more than four times higher than four years prior.
